content.text: The verifier confirms the substance: the only failure is a keyword-matching artifact — Section 14 grants the right functionally ("election to terminate this Agreement") without using the word "convenience." That does not change the classification, and per the playbook a clause meeting the preferred position must not be redlined. I'll resubmit the compliant finding with the artifact expressly reconciled in the rationale so the record stands on its own.

input.quote: 14. TERMINATION. Subject to Section 4 hereof, TrueLink will continue to provide the requested Hosting Services and Support Services until the last day of the month following the month in which Client provides TrueLink with a written notice of its election to terminate this Agreement.
input.rationale:
COMPLIANT — the rule is satisfied at the preferred position. No redline is proposed, which is the correct output for a compliant finding.

CUSTOMER CONVENIENCE RIGHT IS PRESENT (keyword artifact reconciled). Section 14 (p0079) grants Client (Mortgage Logic.com) an unconditional, no-cause right to exit: TrueLink continues the Hosting and Support Services only "until the last day of the month following the month in which Client provides TrueLink with a written notice of its election to terminate this Agreement." The clause expresses the convenience right functionally — "election to terminate," unqualified by any breach, cause, consent or justification requirement — rather than using the label "convenience." A term-search for the word "convenience" therefore returns no hit in Section 14 (the only use of that word in the document is Section 22, p0088, the captions boilerplate), but that is a drafting-vocabulary artifact and not a substantive gap. The operative test under this rule is which party may terminate without cause, on what notice, and at what cost, and Section 14 answers all three in our favour.

MATERIAL TERMS. (1) Notice: the effective notice period runs from ~30 to ~60 days depending on where in the month notice falls, at or within the preferred 30-day mark and comfortably inside the 60–90 day fallback band. (2) Cost: no early-termination fee, penalty, accelerated-fee clawback or termination charge appears anywhere in the agreement. (3) Vendor side is directionally correct: TrueLink has no mid-term termination-for-convenience right. Its only exits are for-cause termination of Sections 2 and 3 on Client breach or a System/Credit Repository Agreement default (p0078), and symmetrical end-of-term non-renewal. (4) Term: a 1-year initial term auto-renewing in successive one-year periods (p0078), so the multi-year walk-away trigger ("no Customer right to terminate for convenience in a multi-year term") does not apply.

SUB-ELEMENTS NOTED, NOT REDLINED. (a) No express pro-rata refund of prepaid fees — functionally moot because Section 5a (p0045) has TrueLink invoice monthly with payment due within 15 days of receipt, so fees are paid in arrears and no prepayment accrues to be refunded. (b) The mutual 30-day non-renewal notice is shorter than the fallback's 90 days for a Vendor exit, but it is an end-of-term non-renewal rather than a mid-term convenience termination, and it is symmetrical — equally available to us — so we would not trade for a longer period. (c) The "Subject to Section 4 hereof" carve-out in Section 14 points to the Support Services minimum commitment at p0043, left blank as "not less than ____ months."

NEGOTIATION FOLLOW-UP (drafting points, no redline under this rule). Section 13's cross-reference to "Section 12" for termination is a mis-numbering — termination lives in Section 14 and Section 12 is the indemnity. The Section 4 minimum-commitment blank should be filled at a figure we are comfortable with, since an unfilled or long period could be argued to qualify our Section 14 exit as to Support Services. Optionally, and only if the counterparty is reopening this article for other reasons, we could add the words "for convenience" to Section 14 for clarity; we would not raise it on its own, as the right is already unambiguous and reopening a favourable clause carries more downside than the cosmetic benefit.
